title: Insights into the renal pathophysiology in Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome-1 from urinary extracellular vesicle proteomics and a new mouse model
description: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome type 1 (HPS-1) is a rare, autosomal recessive disorder caused by defects in the biogenesis of lysosome-related organelles complex-3 (BLOC-3). Impaired kidney function is among its clinical manifestations. To investigate HPS-1 renal involvement, we employed 1D-gel-LC–MS/MS and compared the protein composition of urinary extracellular vesicles (uEVs) from HPS-1 patients to normal control individuals. We identified 1029 proteins, 149 of which were altered in HPS-1 uEVs. Ingenuity Pathway Analysis revealed disruptions in mitochondrial function and the LXR/RXR pathway that regulates lipid metabolism, which is supported by our novel Hps1 knockout mouse. Serum concentration of the LXR/RXR pathway protein ApoA1 in our patient cohort was positively correlated with kidney function (with the estimated glomerular filtration rate or eGFR). uEVs can be used to study epithelial cell protein trafficking in HPS-1 and may provide outcome measures for HPS-1 therapeutic interventions.
sample_protocol: 24-hour urine samples were centrifuged to pellet debris.  The resulting supernatant was centrifuged and treated to remove Tamm-Horsfall protein.  Extracellular vesicle protein lysates were separated by SDS-PAGE; proteins within the bands were reduced, alkylated, and trypsinized; the resulting peptides were extracted.  Peptides were separated and analyzed by a fully automated HPLC-MS/MS system consisting of a Proxeon Easy nLC-II nano-flow high performance liquid chromatography system connected online to an LTQ NSI-Ion Trap mass spectrometer.
data_protocol: Tandem mass spectra were converted to mzML peak list files using ProteoWizard MSconvert and searched against the human subset of the SwissProt database using Mascot Daemon; charge state deconvolution and deisotoping were not performed. Scaffold (version 5.2.0) was used to validate MS/MS based peptide and protein identifications.

title: Multiple reaction monitoring assay for differentiating gastric cancer from acid peptic diseases
description: Gastric cancers (GCs) are often diagnosed in advanced stages, owing to non-specific clinical symptoms at early stages that resemble Acid Peptic Diseases (APDs). Despite recent efforts, a simple, liquid biopsy-based, multi-protein panel pre-diagnostic assay that can differentiate GCs from APDs is lacking. Parallelly, Mass Spectrometry (MS)-based targeted proteomics methods including Multiple Reaction Monitoring (MRM) are being progressively utilised as method-of-choice to build Laboratory Developed Tests (LDTs). An MS-MRM LDT that can quantify a panel of serum proteins was developed and tested in 135 serum samples from treatment-naïve cases of GCs, APDs, and healthy individuals.
sample_protocol: Total Protein Extraction and Sample Preparation for LC-MRM-MS Analysis: Proteins were extracted from 135 serum samples using overnight acetone precipitation. Each 100 µL serum sample was mixed with 500 µL chilled 100% acetone and incubated overnight at -20°C. After centrifugation, supernatants were discarded, and pellets were air-dried and resuspended in 500 µL 100 mM Triethylammonium Bicarbonate (TEAB) buffer. Protein concentration was estimated using the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) on 20 µL of suspension. To normalize sample loading, 10 µg protein from each sample was run on 10% SDS-PAGE. Subsequently, 100 µg of each normalized sample was aliquoted for further processing. Proteins were reduced with 10 mM DTT at 60°C for 30 min, then alkylated with 20 mM iodoacetamide at room temperature for 15 min. Trypsin digestion was performed overnight at 37°C (1:20 enzyme:substrate ratio), followed by quenching with 0.1% formic acid (FA). Digestion efficiency was verified by 10% SDS-PAGE with 1.5 µg equivalent peptides. Samples were desalted using Sep-Pak® C18 Cartridges (Waters), quantified using the Pierce™ Quantitative Peptide Assay, and stored at -20°C until LC-MRM-MS acquisition. Development of LC-MRM-MS-Based Laboratory-Developed Test (LDT) MS Optimization: Proteotypic peptides identified by in-silico analysis were procured from JPT Peptide Technologies (Berlin, Germany), including carbamidomethylated cysteines. Both native (NAT) and stable isotope-labeled (SIS) peptides (labeled at C-terminal R/K with ^13C/^15N) were diluted to 100 pmol/µL. From this stock, working solutions were prepared using 0.1% FA. MS optimization was conducted using 500 fmol/µL NAT peptides via direct infusion into a QTRAP 6500 (SCIEX). Parameters such as Declustering Potential (DP), Entrance Potential (EP), Collision Energy (CE), and Collision Cell Exit Potential (CXP) were optimized per transition. For SIS peptides, the same parameters were used except for m/z. At least two transitions were optimized per peptide precursor. LC Optimization: LC separation was optimized using pooled peptides (500 fmol/µL) on an Agilent 1290 Infinity II UHPLC system. Parameters such as solvent gradient, column temperature, and injection volume were tested. A ZORBAX RRHD Eclipse Plus C18 column (2.1 × 50 mm, 1.8 µm, 95Å) was used. Mobile phases included 0.1% FA (A) and 90% acetonitrile in 0.1% FA (B). The reverse-phase gradient used a 250 µL/min flow rate, 10 µL injection volume, and 35°C column temperature. All 11 peptides (NAT and SIS) were resolved; co-eluting peptides showed a retention time difference of 0.1 min. Preparation of Calibration Standards, QC Samples, and Method Validation Calibration Standards: Each peptide was serially diluted into 9 concentrations (500–1.95 fmol/µL) using 0.1% FA. SIS peptides (500 fmol/µL) served as internal standards (IS) for all concentrations. A blank standard (0.1% FA + IS) was included. Pooled mixes created 10 calibration standards, each run in triplicate using the optimized LC-MRM-MS method. QC Samples: QC samples were prepared by pooling 15 µg equivalent peptides from all 135 serum samples. These pooled QCs matched validation concentrations and were used both for method validation and during LC-MRM-MS analysis. QC Stability: QC stability was tested after 6 and 24 h incubation at -20°C and 4°C (autosampler) with IS at 500 fmol/µL. Each sample was run in triplicate. Method Validation: Carryover was assessed by analyzing 500 fmol/µL SIS peptides followed by blanks, repeated thrice. Matrix effects were evaluated by spiking pooled SIS peptides into either sample matrix or 0.1% FA at both high (500 fmol/µL) and low (50 fmol/µL) concentrations. Retention time (RT) shifts were monitored to assess matrix impact. LC-MRM-MS Analysis of Serum Samples: Peptides from 135 serum samples were analyzed by LC-MRM-MS using strict QC and randomization protocols. Nine acquisition batches were run; each included 15 samples (5 each from GC, APD, HI groups) and 4 QCs. All samples were spiked with SIS peptides at 166.6 fmol/µL (mid-calibration range) and analyzed in triplicate. Quality control included intra-day, inter-day, and batch-level checks to ensure reproducibility.
data_protocol: The Skyline software  was utilized for data analysis, including RT alignment, peak picking, normalization and quantification (RRID:SCR_014080). Calibration curves were plotted for each peptide using linear regression fit with 1/x2 weighing. SIS peptide intensities were used as IS for data normalization. Accurate and precise measurements of calibration standards were carried out with a maximum of 20% LOQ bias. A maximum of 20% CV was allowed for determining LOQ for every peptide. LOD was determined as Blank+3*Standard Deviation. To calculate the stability of QC samples, CV was calculated for all 4 incubation conditions (maximum peak height %CV<30%; RT %CV<20%). Matrix effect was calculated as %CV of RT of each peptide with and without matrix at higher and lower concentrations (%CV<20%). Carryover was calculated by comparing peak intensity of spike-in standard to following blank. Difference between intensities was calculated as ratio of peak intensities. A threshold of 20 times higher signal than blank corresponded to minimal carryover. Finally, LC-MRM-MS data of serum samples and batch QC were imported into Skyline (RRID:SCR_014080). Quantification and RT data were used for further processing. A threshold of %CV<20% was considered for QC measurement consistency/variation. Peptides showing conserved RT alignment among samples were chosen for final protein quantification. Quantification data was utilized for further statistical and functional analysis.

title: Challenging the Astral mass analyzer – up to 5300 proteins per single-cell at unseen quantitative accuracy to study cellular heterogeneity.
description: This is an additional dataset to PXD049412 A detailed proteome map is crucial for understanding molecular pathways and protein functions. Despite significant advancements in sample preparation, instrumentation, and data analysis, single-cell proteomics is currently limited by proteomic depth and quantitative performance. We combine a zero dead-end volume chromatographic column running at high throughput with the Thermo Scientific™ Orbitrap™ Astral™ mass spectrometer running in DIA mode. We yield unprecedented depth of proteome coverage as well as accuracy and precision for quantification of ultra-low input amounts. Using a tailored library, we identify up to 7400 protein groups from as little as 250 pg HeLa at a throughput of 50 samples per day (SPD). We benchmark multiple data analysis strategies, estimate their influence on FDR and show that FDR on protein level can easily be maintained at 1 %. Using a two-proteome mix, we check for optimal parameters of quantification and show that fold change differences of 2 can still be successfully determined at single-cell level inputs. Eventually, we apply our workflow to A549 cells yielding a proteome coverage of up to 5200 protein groups from a single cell, which allows the observation of heterogeneity in a cellular population and studying dependencies between cell size and cell-cycle phase. Additionally, our workflow enables us to distinguish between in vitro analogs of two human blastocyst lineages: naïve human pluripotent stem cells (epiblast) and trophectoderm (TE)-like cells. Gene Ontology analysis of enriched proteins in TE-like cells harmoniously aligns with transcriptomic data, indicating that single-cell proteomics possesses the capability to identify biologically relevant differences between these two lineages within the blastocyst.
sample_protocol: A549 and HeLa cell isolation, lysis and digestion was performed within a 384-well plate (Thermo Scientific™ Armadillo 45PCR Plate, 384-well, # 12657516) using the cellenONE® robot. Cells were sorted into wells containing 1µL of master mix (0.2% n-dodecyl-beta-maltoside (D4641-500MG, Sigma Aldrich, Germany), 100mM tetraethylammonium bicarbonate (17902-500ML, Fluka Analytical, Switzer-land), 3ng/µL trypsin (Trypsin Gold, V5280, Promega, USA) and 0.01% enhancer (ProteaseMAX, V2071, Promega, USA) and 1 % DMSO). For single cell samples, cells were deposited into individual wells, while for 20x or 40x libraries, the respective cell-number was sorted into a single well. Humidity and temperature were controlled at 50% and 15°C during cell sorting. A549 cells were isolated at given diameter of 15-30 µm and HeLa cells at 18-25 μm. The maximum elongation was set to 1.5. Cell lysis and protein digestion were done at 50°C and 85% relative humidity for 30 min before an additional 500nL of 3ng/μL trypsin were added. After lysis and digestion, 3.5 μL of 0.1% TFA were added to the respective wells for quenching and storage at -20°C. For the LC-MS/MS analysis, samples were directly injected from the 384 well plate.
data_protocol: All raw-data was analyzed using Spectronaut (v 18.6.231227.55695, Biognosys AG). For results marked as “Method Evaluation”, directDIA+ was used in method evaluation mode without cross normalization and with every raw file defined as separate condition to ensure Spectronaut treats each file like it they were analyzed in-dividually. “Direct DIA+ with matching” indicates results analyzed in directDIA+ mode with replicates defined as same condition in the search settings. For library searches higher input DIA recorded results (as given) were first analyzed in direct DIA+ mode and a library was created from those files using Spectronaut. Quantification was performed on MS1 level. Carbamidomethylation of cysteines as a static modification was removed for single-cell searches as no alkylation step was performed. Besides that, factory settings were used for all analyses and for library generation. Searches were performed against the human proteome (uniprot prote-ome UP000005640, reviewed, 20408 protein entries, downloaded 4th Aug 2023) and the crapome37 (118 protein entries). Searches for the two-proteome analysis were run against the same human database and the yeast prote-ome (UniProt proteome UP0000023116050, reviewed, 6727 protein entries, downloaded 11th Dec. 2023).

title: IsoBayes: a Bayesian approach for single-isoform proteomics inference
description: The dataset in this Proteome Exchange entry are specific to the WTC11 benchmarking samples described in the "IsoBayes" publication (Bollon et al.) Motivation: Studying protein isoforms is an essential step in biomedical research; at present, the main approach for analyzing proteins is via bottom-up mass spectrometry proteomics, which return peptide identifications, that are indirectly used to infer the presence of protein isoforms. However, the detection and quantification processes are noisy; in particular, peptides may be erroneously detected, and most peptides, known as shared peptides, are associated to multiple protein isoforms. As a consequence, studying individual protein isoforms is challenging, and inferred protein results are often abstracted to the gene-level or to groups of protein isoforms.  Results: Here, we introduce IsoBayes, a novel statistical method to perform inference at the isoform level. Our method enhances the information available, by integrating mass spectrometry proteomics and transcriptomics data in a Bayesian probabilistic framework. To account for the uncertainty in the measurement process, we propose a two-layer latent variable approach: first, we sample if a peptide has been correctly detected (or, alternatively filter peptides); second, we allocate the abundance of such selected peptides across the protein(s) they are compatible with. This enables us, starting from peptide-level data, to recover protein-level data; in particular, we: i) infer the presence/absence of each protein isoform (via a posterior probability), ii) estimate its abundance (and credible interval), and iii) target isoforms where transcript and protein relative abundances significantly differ. We benchmarked our approach in simulations, and in two multi-protease real datasets: our method displays good sensitivity and specificity when detecting protein isoforms, its estimated abundances highly correlate with the ground truth, and can detect changes between protein and transcript relative abundances.  Availability and implementation: IsoBayes is freely distributed as a Bioconductor R package, and is accompanied by an example usage vignette.

title: Integrating Alternative Fragmentation Techniques into Standard LC-MS Workflows Using a Single Deep Learning Model Enhances Proteome Coverage
description: We built and characterised a mass spectrometer capable of performing CID (both beam type and resonant type), UVPD, EID and ECD in an automated fashion during an LCMS type experiment. We exploited this ability to generate large datasets through multienzyme deep proteomics experiments for characterisation of these activation techniques. As a further step, motivated by the complexity generated by these dissociation techniques, we developed a single Prosit deep learning model for fragment ion intensity prediction covering all of these techniques. The generated model has been made publicly available and has been utilised in FragPipe within its MSBooster module. Rescoring allowed both data-dependent acquisition (DDA) and data-independent acquisition (DIA) to achieve on average more than 10% increase in protein identifications across all dissociation techniques and enzymatic digestions. We demonstrate that these alternative fragmentation approaches can now be used within standard data analysis pipelines and can produce data competitive to CID in terms of eficiency, but in the cases of EID and UVPD with far richer and more comprehensive spectra.
sample_protocol: Reagents, including SDS, DMSO, TEAB, urea, and acetonitrile, were used for cell lysis and protein solubilization. Proteins from human Expi293F, Arabidopsis thaliana, and E. coli were extracted and subjected to sonication, reduction with TCEP, and alkylation with CAA. Protein concentration was measured using a BCA assay. For Arabidopsis, the protocol included PVPP beads, protease/phosphatase inhibitors, and clarification by centrifugation. Digestion strategies varied by protease: trypsin, LysC, and LysN utilized a modified SP3 protocol involving magnetic carboxyl-coated beads and acetonitrile-induced precipitation; chymotrypsin digestion required dilution and organic solvent washes; GluC digestion followed urea dilution. All peptide mixtures were acidified, desalted on Oasis HLB cartridges, and dried. Expi293F digests were fractionated by UPLC using a gradient of acetonitrile in TEAB buffer and pooled into 20 final fractions. LC-MS/MS analysis was carried out on Orbitrap-based platforms with various dissociation methods (HCD, ETciD, EID, UVPD, ECD) using DDA or (EID, UVPD, ECD) using DIA modes. DIA used staggered isolation windows over extended gradients depending on mass ranges and fragmentation strategy. Peptide separation was performed on nanoLC with custom-packed C18 columns. Injection amounts varied by protease and method, with typical MS1 acquisition settings including high-resolution scans, AGC control, and defined injection times tailored for each fragmentation technique.
data_protocol: For DDA datasets, spectra were searched using FragPipe (v22.0) with MSFragger 4.1, applying a standard close search strategy against the UniProt Homo sapiens database (accessed 24.10.29). Fragment ion types were adjusted based on the fragmentation method, including user-defined ions (a+1, c−1, x+1, z+1) for compatibility. Searches for GluC and chymotrypsin allowed up to four missed cleavages. Filtering of search results was performed using Percolator (v3.6.5), Philosopher (v5.1.1), and ProteinProphet, with results reported using sequential FDR estimation at 1% protein-level FDR. Rescoring was performed using the Oktoberfest tool in combination with Percolator on 100% FDR search results. For DIA datasets, FragPipe (v23.0) with MSFragger-DIA 4.1.52 was used with the ‘DIA_SpecLib_Quant’ settings, searching against organism-specific UniProt databases for Homo sapiens, Arabidopsis thaliana, and E. coli (accessed in 2022).  Peptide property predictions (iRT and intensity) were generated via MSBooster using the “Prosit_2019_irt” and “Prosit_2025_intensity_MultiFrag” models implemented in Koina. Filtering of DIA search results was conducted using Percolator (v3.7.1) and Philosopher (v5.1.1), with FDR control applied at the levels of PSMs, peptides, and proteins (1% for each).

title: A proteomics data of 30 tissues in aging female rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta)
description: A systematic investigation of aging patterns across virtually all major tissues in non-human primates, our evolutionarily closest relatives, can provide valuable insights into tissue aging in humans, which is still elusive largely due to the difficulty in sampling. Here, we generated and analyzed multi-omics data, including transcriptome, proteome, and metabolome, from 30 tissues of 17 female rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) aged 3 to 27 years. We found that certain molecular features, such as increased inflammation, are consistent across tissues and align with findings in mice and humans. We further revealed that tissue aging in macaques is asynchronous and can be classified into two distinct types, with one type exhibiting more pronounced aging degree, likely associated with decreased mRNA translation efficiency, and predominantly contributing to whole-body aging. This work provides a comprehensive molecular landscape of aging in non-human primate tissues and links translation efficiency to tissue-specific aging.
sample_protocol: Total protein extraction: Solid tissue samples were individually ground in liquid nitrogen and lysed using DB lysis buffer (100 mM TEAB, 8 M urea, pH 8.5). This was followed by 5 minutes of ultrasonication on ice. The lysate was then centrifuged at 12 000 g for 15 minutes at 4°C. The supernatant was reduced with 10 mM DTT for 1 hour at 56°C, and subsequently alkylated with iodoacetamide for 1 hour in the dark. Protein quality test: Following the Bradford Protein Quantitative Kit instructions, a BSA standard protein solution was prepared with gradient concentrations ranging from 0 to 0.5 g/L. Both the BSA standard solutions and variously diluted sample solutions were added to a 96-well plate, each at a volume of 20 µL. Each gradient was tested in triplicate. We then swiftly added 180 µL of G250 dye solution to each well and allowed it to react at room temperature for 5 minutes. Absorbance was measured at 595 nm. A standard curve was generated, from which the absorbance of the standard protein solution and the protein concentration of the samples were calculated. For protein analysis, 20 μg of each sample was loaded onto a 12% SDS-PAGE gel. The stacking gel was run at 80 V for 20 minutes, followed by the resolving gel at 120 V for 90 minutes. The gel was subsequently stained with Coomassie Brilliant Blue R-250 and destained until the protein bands were clearly visible. Trypsin treatment: The volume of the protein samples was adjusted to 100 μL using DB lysis buffer (100 mM TEAB, 8 M urea, pH 8.5). Trypsin and 100 mM TEAB buffer were then added, and the mixture was incubated at 37°C for 4 hours for digestion. Additional trypsin and CaCl2 were introduced for an overnight digestion. The digested sample was acidified with formic acid (FA) to a pH of less than 3 and centrifuged at 12,000 g for 5 minutes at room temperature. The supernatant was carefully loaded onto a C18 desalting column, washed three times with a washing buffer containing 0.1% FA and 3% acetonitrile (ACN), and then eluted with a buffer containing 0.1% FA and 70% ACN. The eluates from each sample were collected and freeze-dried.
data_protocol: Data-dependent acquisition (DDA) spectral library construction Separation of fractions: To develop a gradient elution, mobile phase A (2% ACN, pH 10.0 with ammonium hydroxide) and mobile phase B (98% ACN, pH 10.0 with ammonium hydroxide) were utilized. The lyophilized powder was dissolved in solution A and centrifuged at 12 000 g for 10 minutes at room temperature. Fractionation of the sample was performed on a Rigol L3000 HPLC system, with the column oven maintained at 45°C. Eluates were monitored at 214 nm UV, and subsequently combined into 10 fractions. All fractions were then dried under vacuum and reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid (FA) in water. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis for DDA mode: To construct the transition library, we conducted shotgun proteomics analyses using an EASY-nLCTM 1200 UHPLC system paired with a Q-ExactiveTM HF-X mass spectrometer in DDA mode using the default setting. A sample containing 4 μg of fraction supernatant and 0.8 μL of iRT reagent was injected into a custom-made C18 Nano-Trap column (4.5 cm × 75 μm, 3 μm). Peptides were then separated on a custom-made analytical column (15 cm × 150 μm, 1.9 μm) using a linear gradient elution. The separated peptides were analyzed with the Q-ExactiveTM HF-X mass spectrometer, utilizing the Nanospray Flex™ ion source. The scan range was set as from 350 m/z to 1 500 m/z with a resolution of 120,000. The 40 most abundant precursors from the scan were selected for fragmentation and analyzed. The raw MS detection data were then used to build the DDA spectral library. LC-MS/MS analysis-data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode: The data-independent acquisition (DIA) mode of LC-MS/MS was conducted using an EASY-nLC™ 1200 UHPLC system coupled with an Orbitrap Q-Exactive™ HF-X mass spectrometer operating in DIA mode. The system was configured with a spray voltage of 2.1 kV, Nanospray Flex™ (ESI), and a capillary temperature of 320°C. For DIA acquisition, the m/z range was set from 350 to 1,500. The MS1 resolution was configured to 60,000, with a full scan AGC target value of 5 × 105 and a maximum ion injection time of 20 ms. Peptides were fragmented by HCD in MS2, where the resolution was set to 30,000, and the AGC target value was set to 1 × 106, and the normalized collision energy was set to 27%. Identification and quantitation of protein: For each tissue sample, the spectra derived from each fraction were independently processed using the Proteome Discoverer v2.2 (PD v2.2, Thermo) software. The search criteria were defined with a precursor ion mass tolerance of 10 ppm and a product ion mass tolerance of 0.02 Da. Carbamidomethylation was designated as a constant modification, while methionine oxidation was treated as a variable modification, and N-terminal acetylation was specified as a modification in PD v2.2. To enhance the reliability of the analysis, PD v2.2 was utilized to further filter the search outcomes: i) Peptide Spectrum Matches (PSMs) with a confidence level exceeding 99% were considered identified PSMs; ii) Identified proteins were required to have at least one unique peptide; and iii) Identified PSMs and proteins were retained with a false discovery rate (FDR) not exceeding 1.0%.  For the multi-tissue omics analysis, the search and identification results from PD v2.2 were imported into Spectronaut (Biognosys) to create a comprehensive library. Peptides and product ions were selected based on specific rules to generate a target list. The DIA data were then imported, and chromatographic peaks of ion pairs were extracted according to this target list. The ions and their calculated peak areas were matched to identify and quantify peptides. Protein quantification was determined as the average of the top three peptides. The iRT reagent was added to the samples to correct retention times, and the precursor ion Q-value cutoff was set at 0.01. The “SNE Combine Workflow” in Spectronaut was utilized to conduct a combined analysis of all tissues. The MS status file was filtered using a Q-value threshold of less than 0.01.

title: Enhancing Peptide Identification in Metaproteomics through Curriculum Learning in Deep Learning
description: Metaproteomics offers a powerful window into the active functions of microbial communities, but accurately identifying peptides remains challenging due to the size and incompleteness of protein databases derived from metagenomes. These databases often contain vastly more sequences than those from single organisms, creating a computational bottleneck in peptide-spectrum match (PSM) filtering. Here we present WinnowNet, a deep learning–based method for PSM filtering, available in two versions: one using transformers and the other convolutional neural networks. Both variants are designed to handle the unordered nature of PSM data and are trained using a curriculum learning strategy that moves from simple to complex examples. WinnowNet consistently achieves more true identifications at equivalent false discovery rates compared to leading tools, including Percolator, MS$^2$Rescore, and DeepFilter, and outperforms filters integrated into popular analysis pipelines. It also uncovers more gut microbiome biomarkers related to diet and health, highlighting its potential to support advances in personalized medicine
sample_protocol: For the ProteomeTools dataset, dried peptide pools were solubilized in 100% DMSO to a concentration of 10 pmol/ul by vortexing for 30 minutes at room temperature, then diluted to 10% DMSO with 1% formic acid in HPLC-grade water. Approximately 200 fmol of each peptide was analyzed using a Dionex 3000 HPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The LC system was directly coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Each peptide pool was analyzed with a full MS scan in the Orbitrap at a resolution of 60,000, followed by HCD MS/MS scans at 28% normalized collision energy (resolution 15,000), and CID scans at 35% normalized collision energy. For the marine and soil datasets, peptide samples were loaded into the column using a pressure cell. The column was equilibrated with HPLC Solvent A (5% acetonitrile, 95% H2O, 0.1% formic acid), followed by separation on an analytical column containing 15~cm of C18 RP media. Mass spectrometry analysis was performed using an LTQ Orbitrap Elite instrument (Thermo Scientific). Tandem mass spectra were acquired across 11 consecutive online SCX fractions, with MS1 and MS2 scans recorded at resolutions of 30000 and 15000, respectively. For the human gut dataset, fecal samples were suspended in 45mL of phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), vortexed for 45 minutes, and centrifuged at 500 xg for 5 minutes to remove food debris. Proteins were extracted, alkylated with iodoacetamide (IAA), and digested overnight with trypsin. The resulting peptides were purified and concentrated using Pierce C18 spin columns (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and quantified via the Pierce Quantitative Colorimetric Peptide Assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were analyzed on an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to a Nano ACQUITY UPLC system. Full MS scans were acquired at a resolution of 120000, followed by HCD MS/MS scans at a resolution of 30000.
data_protocol: The MS data was searched using Comet, MS-GF+, Myrimatch and filtered by Percolator, MS2Rescore, Q-ranker, PeptideProphet, iProphet, DeepFilter and WinnowNet. The precursor and fragment mass tolerances were set to 0.09 Da and 0.01 Da, respectively. Peptides within the mass range of 700 to 7000 Da were considered. Trypsin/P was selected as the proteolytic enzyme, with a maximum allowance of three missed cleavages.

title: LFQ Benchmark Dataset - Generation Beta: Assessing Modern Proteomics Instruments and Acquisition Workflows with High-Throughput LC Gradients
description: Recent advancements in liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) have increasingly focused on high-throughput workflows, leveraging rapid chromatographic gradients and minimal sample input to maximize proteome coverage from limited material. This shift is particularly driven by the rise of single-cell proteomics, where sensitivity and reproducibility are critical. Building on our previous benchmark dataset (PXD028735), we now present an expanded study utilizing the latest generation of LC-MS platforms optimized for high-throughput proteomics. This study features shorter LC gradients and lower sample input to address the growing need for rapid and sensitive proteome analysis. Using a standardized hybrid proteome mixture with defined ratios of Human, Yeast, and E. coli, we generated a comprehensive Data-Dependent and Data-Independent Acquisition (DDA/DIA) dataset across multiple state-of-the-art LC-MS platforms. The updated dataset incorporates the latest acquisition methodologies and extends coverage across an even broader range of data formats, including enhanced ion mobility-enabled and scanning quadrupole-based acquisitions. Our results providea detailed assessment of the impact of technological advancements and demonstrate how shortening LC gradients influence proteome coverage, quantitative precision, and data consistency across instruments
sample_protocol: Mass spectrometry-compatible protein digest extracts from Human K562 (P/N: V6951, Lot: 0000608712) and Yeast (P/N: V7461, Lot: 0000601330) were obtained from Promega (Madison, Wisconsin, USA), while the lyophilized MassPrep Escherichia coli digest standard (P/N: 186003196, Lot: W01111913) was sourced from Waters Corporation (Milford, Massachusetts, USA). Each extract underwent reduction with dithiothreitol (DTT), alkylation with iodoacetamide (IAA), and digestion with sequencing grade Trypsin (-Lys C) according to the manufacturers' protocols. The digested protein extracts were reconstituted in a solution of 0.1% formic acid (FA) in 5% acetonitrile (Biosolve B.V, Valkenswaard, The Netherlands). Following the approach of Navarro et al., two master samples, A and B, were prepared as illustrated in Figure 1. Sample A consisted of Human, Yeast, and E. coli digests mixed at 65%, 30%, and 5% weight/weight (w/w), respectively. Sample B was formulated by combining Human, Yeast, and E. coli protein digests at 65%, 15%, and 20% w/w, respectively. Additionally, a third mixture, Sample C, was created with Human, Yeast, and E. coli protein digests at 65%, 3%, and 32% w/w, respectively, to assess the impact of larger ratio differences on analytical performance.
data_protocol: The 15-min 50 ng nanoflow DIA datasets for Conditions A and B (n = 12) were analysed with DIA-NN (v2.1.0) in library-free mode, using a FASTA database comprising UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot protein sequences from Homo sapiens, Escherichia coli, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae, combined with a universal contaminant protein database. Trypsin/P was selected as the proteolytic enzyme, allowing up to one missed cleavage, and precursor ion charge states from +1 to +5 were considered.

title: Single-cell proteomic landscape of the developing human brain
description: The label free single cell proteome profiling in developing human brain.
sample_protocol:
Tissue samples for proteomic profiling were dissociated using the Papain Dissociation System (Worthington, LK003150). Neuronal cells were sorted by FACS using a Sony SH800 (100-µm nozzle). Live cells were collected as single cells and deposited into 384-well low-bind PCR plates. Each well was pre-loaded with 1 µL of lysis buffer consisting of 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (TEAB, pH 8.5), 10 mM tris(2-carboxyethyl)phosphine (TCEP), 40 mM chloroacetamide (CAA), and 0.1% n-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside (DDM). After sorting, plates were centrifuged briefly at 1000 × g for 1 min to collect contents at the bottom of the wells, then sealed with a heat-resistant adhesive aluminum film, snap-frozen on dry ice, and stored at −80 °C to preserve protein integrity until processing.
      For protein extraction, plates were thawed on ice and incubated at 95 °C for 5 min in a Bio-Rad 384-well thermal cycler, with the lid set to 105 °C to minimize condensation and maximize lysis efficiency. After cooling to room temperature, 1 µL of enzyme solution containing 2.5 ng sequencing-grade trypsin was added to each well, bringing the final digestion volume to 2 µL per well.   Digestion was carried out overnight at 37 °C in the thermocycler, with plates continuously sealed using adhesive aluminum film to prevent evaporation during the extended incubation.  Following digestion, reactions were quenched by adding 1 µL of 2% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) to adjust the pH to approximately 3, thereby inactivating trypsin and stabilizing the peptides for downstream analysis. Samples were then manually loaded onto EvoTip Pure devices using an electronic multichannel pipette in parallel across wells for desalting and sample cleanup. This step was performed according to the Evosep loading protocol with a standardized SOP, which we used to minimize operator variability. The peptides bound to the tips were subsequently subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis using an optimized gradient for low-input proteomics. This workflow enabled robust and reproducible peptide recovery from individual cells, providing the foundation for label-free single-cell proteomic profiling of the developing human brain.
data_protocol: Single-cell proteomic data were processed with DIA-NN against the UniProt human reference proteome (Trypsin/P; up to two missed cleavages; peptide length 7–30 aa; precursor charge 1–4). Fixed and variable modifications included carbamidomethylation (C, fixed), methionine oxidation (variable), and allowance for N-terminal methionine excision. Mass accuracy tolerances were set to 5 ppm (MS1) and 10 ppm (MS2). Precursor, peptide, and protein identifications were controlled at 1% FDR. Quantification used fragment-ion peak areas aggregated to precursors and then to proteins, with match-between-runs (MBR) enabled. Protein groups were mapped to UniProt IDs and corresponding gene symbols prior to downstream analysis.

title: Glycoproteome-Wide Discovery of Cortical Glycoproteins That May Provide Cognitive Resilience in Older Adults
description: Background and Objectives  Molecular omics studies have identified proteins related to cognitive resilience but unrelated to Alzheimer disease and Alzheimer disease–related dementia (AD/ADRD) pathologies. Posttranslational modifications of proteins with glycans can modify protein function. In this study, we identified glycopeptiforms associated with cognitive resilience. Methods  We studied brains from adults with annual cognitive testing with postmortem indices of 10 AD/ADRD pathologies and proteome-wide data from dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). We quantified 11, 012 glycopeptiforms from DLPFC using liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry. We used linear mixed-effects models to identify glycopeptiforms associated with cognitive decline correcting for multiple comparisons (p < 5 × 10−6). Then, we regressed out the effect of AD/ADRD pathologies to identify glycopeptiforms that may provide cognitive resilience.
sample_protocol: Tissue lysis Glycoproteome-wide study was conducted on frozen DLPFC samples.15 Brain tissue was transferred to 2 mL bead-beating tubes (Precellys lysing kit p000918-LYSK0-A), and 500 μL of 5% SDS in 50 mM Tris buffer was added to the tubes. The samples were homogenized using a Bead Beater (PRECELLYS Evolution, Bertin Technologies) for 10 s at 10 000 rpm, 6 s pause, and 1 min on ice, three times. Then three cycles of 20 s, 6800 rpm, and 30 s pause between cycles were carried out. The tubes were then transferred to a benchtop centrifuge at 13 000g for 10 min at 4 °C. The supernatant fluid was transferred to new Eppendorf tubes and frozen at −80 °C. Lysates were mixed vol:vol with 10% SDS, 50 mM Tris, pH 7.55, for a total volume of 50 μL. The samples were heated for 15 min at 96 °C with 500 rpm rotation and then sonicated for 10 cycles (Bioraptor Pico, Diagnode) and centrifuged for 8 min at 13 000g. S-trap digestion Total protein concentration was measured using a BCA assay. One hundred micrograms of each sample was used for downstream preparation. Dithiothreitol (DTT) was prepared fresh in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and added to a final concentration of 5 mM. Samples were then incubated at 56 °C for 1 h. Iodoacetamide was prepared fresh in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and added to a final concentration of 10 mM. Samples were incubated in the dark for 45 min. Phosphoric acid was then added to the samples to a final concentration of 1%. The samples were mixed with 350 μL of 90% MeOH + 10% 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate and then transferred to the S-trap cartridge (Protifi, USA), centrifuged for 1 min at 4000g, washed three times with 400 μL of 90% MeOH + 10% 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, and then centrifuged at 4000g for 1 6 min. Four microliters of 0.5 μg/μL trypsin in 125 μL in ammonium bicarbonate (50:1 protein amount:trypsin) was added to the samples. Samples were incubated at 37 °C overnight. The next day, peptides were eluted using 80 μL of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, which was added to the S-trap cartridge and centrifuged at 4000g for 1 min into new tubes, and the peptides were then collected. Then, a second digestion was performed using 4 μL of 0.5 μg/μL trypsin in 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate, which was added to the eluted samples and incubated at 37 °C for 4 h. Two more elations from the S-trap cartridge were performed: one was carried out with 80 μL of 0.2% formic acid, which was added to the S-trap cartridge and spun down at 4000g for 1 min. The second was done using 80 μL of 50% acetonitrile + 0.2% formic acid, which was added to the cartridge and spun down at 4000g for 1 min. The three elutions were mixed and dried using a vacuum centrifuge (Centrivac, LabConco). Glycopeptide enrichment Twenty microliters of in-house derivatized beads15 (per sample) were spun down to remove storage buffers and washed with the loading buffer twice. Samples were dissolved in 50 μL of loading buffer (50% MeCN, 50mM bicarbonate-carbonate buffer pH 10.5, 1M KCl) and added to the beads. Beads were incubated in rotation at RT for 30 min, and the beads were then loaded on empty 10ul TopTips (Glygen Inc) and spun in a centrifuge at 376g for 30 s to remove the solution. Beads were washed twice with the loading buffer and twice with the washing buffer (50% MeCN, 50mM bicarbonate-carbonate buffer pH 10.5). Twenty microliters of 5% formic acid/50%ACN was added to the samples, incubated for 10 min at RT to elute the bound glycopeptides. The samples were spun for 60 s. The above volume of elution buffer was added again and eluted immediately.
data_protocol: Raw data was searched using Byonic search engine16 against the human proteome database, and an in-house 182 glycan library for the brain samples. Resulting identifications were filtered for 1% and a minimum Byonic score of 300 for increased stringency.17 Glycopeptides were quantified using FlashLFQ standalone GUI version using default settings with normalization and ‘match between runs’ enabled
